summary: Moonwalker helps people decide where and when to land on the Moon. Mission teams use the Planner: they pick a site, a landing date, a lander and a set of requirements, and the first screen says whether the plan works and, if the site or date has to move, where the nearest alternative is. It shows the Sun and Earth against the real terrain horizon, when each one next sets, and every window in the year with both sunlight and a direct link to Earth. Further pages cover battery survival through dark spans, ground-station contact, landing-ellipse statistics and launch-slip analysis. Everyone else uses Explorer, where you can walk or drive a rover at Apollo 11, Blue Ghost, Chang’e 4 and two spots at Shackleton crater, watch the light and shadows change, and take five short lessons on why sunlight and Earth in the sky decide where a lander can work. Our own engine computes every number from NASA SPICE ephemerides and LOLA terrain, and we check it against outside references: 43 of 46 checks pass. The two modes share that engine and link to each other, so a planner’s site can be explored in 3D and an Explorer site can be analysed in the Planner.
details:
What it does

Moonwalker answers one question for a lunar landing: if the landing site or date moves, is the mission still viable, and what is the nearest alternative?

The Planner is for mission teams. A plan panel holds four choices: the site (click the map or type coordinates), the landing time, the lander and the requirements. The Overview shows a verdict for the plan, the Sun and Earth paths against the terrain horizon at the site, the time to the next sunset or Earthset, and a year strip with every landing date that meets the requirements. The Site page has the full analysis: sunlight and Earth-link timelines, battery state through dark spans, contact with the Deep Space Network stations, and statistics over the landing ellipse. Map finds sites in an area, and Compare puts several sites against several dates in one grid. Results export as CSV, JSON, CCSDS attitude files and HTML or PDF mission reports.

Explorer is for students, teachers and the public. You can walk as an astronaut or drive a rover at three past landing sites (Apollo 11, Blue Ghost and Chang’e 4) and at two south-pole spots on the rim and floor of Shackleton crater. The hardware that was really left at each site is there, such as the Apollo 11 descent stage, flag, seismometer and laser reflector, each with a short fact card and its source. Time can be played or scrubbed to watch the Sun move and shadows sweep across the ground. Other views show the scene from space, the sky from the ground, and the whole of Shackleton crater in 3D. Five lessons cover why a lunar day lasts a month, why Earth stays in one spot in the sky, why the Sun stays low at the pole, rim versus floor, and why the landing date matters. Rover missions let you repeat the tasks of the last five rovers that worked on the Moon (Yutu, Yutu-2, Pragyan, SORA-Q and Jinchan). “Analyse in Planner” sends the place you are standing to the Planner, and “Stand here in Explorer” lets you walk a planned site on its laser-map ground at the planned landing time.

How it works

The engine is written in Python. It uses NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440) for the positions of the Sun, Earth and the ground stations, and builds terrain stores from LOLA global and polar DEMs, the 5 m PGDA south-pole site models and SLDEM2015. For each site it computes a horizon profile, treats the Sun as a disc with limb darkening to get the visible fraction, and runs power, battery and link budgets over the stay. Each result carries its terrain uncertainty. A FastAPI service runs the long analyses in a job pool. The web app is React and TypeScript, with three.js for the 3D views.

Validation is part of the product. An oracle suite compares the engine with values it did not produce, including JPL Horizons, NASA’s published illumination and Earth-visibility maps, LRO NAC images, laser-ranging data and the recorded times of real missions. Every tolerance is written down before the run, and misses stay in the score. The latest run passes 43 of 46 checks, and the Evidence page shows the results and the misses.

An optional analysis agent answers planning questions in plain language. It calls the engine through typed tools and keeps a ledger of every number it cites. It runs in a sandbox and is off by default.

Who it helps and why it matters

Tools like Quickmap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons hold this information, but comparing site and date options in them takes many steps. Moonwalker gives a planner a verdict and the nearest alternative on the first screen, which helps when a launch slips or a site turns out to be poor. For the public, Explorer shows why the south pole is hard: the floor of Shackleton never sees the Sun, while the rim is lit most of the time.

Tools and technology

Python, NumPy, SciPy, Numba, SpiceyPy, rasterio, FastAPI and WeasyPrint for the engine and service; React, TypeScript, Vite, three.js and zustand for the web app; uv and bun for builds; Docker on a Google Cloud VM, with the terrain stores in a public Cloud Storage bucket. 3D models of the landers, rovers, cockpit and solar panel are generated as GLB files by scripts in the repository. Claude Code helped write the code (see the AI use answer).

What is creative about it

The same engine serves two audiences through two doors, and the two modes hand a site back and forth. Explorer turns the engineering question into something you can feel: drive into a crater and watch your solar panel stop charging. An “Is this real?” note on every view says what is measured, what is simplified and what is made up for the visit (for example, the astronaut and rover were not there, and the lamps on the crater floor are pretend).

What we considered

Honesty about accuracy shaped most decisions. Numbers show their uncertainty, the validation results include the failures, and Explorer marks every simplification. We also wanted it to work for different people and devices. Controls stay folded until you need them, everything works by keyboard, phones get touch controls, and Explorer still runs without the analysis server.
